saint_pick.name: Willehad of Bremen
saint_pick.selection_reason: Willehad, the Northumbrian missionary to the Frisians and Saxons, is well documented in the near-contemporary Vita Willehadi, and his story is vivid: at Dokkum a sword blow aimed at his neck was said to be turned aside by the small reliquary hanging there, and later he fled as the Saxon revolt killed his fellow missionaries. This also gives a Carolingian-era, northern European setting after a week of Roman, Italian and Welsh saints, whereas the Four Crowned Martyrs would be one more early Roman martyr story.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Canonized by pre-congregation cult. Listed in the Roman Martyrology on 8 November as first Bishop of Bremen and Apostle of Saxony. Kept as a feast in the local calendars of the German dioceses of Hamburg, Osnabrück and Hildesheim, and in the Bremen region.

beats.text: Again and again, people tried to kill him. He kept coming back.
beats.scene: An icon of Saint Willehad as an eighth-century missionary in a plain traveling cloak, standing with a staff at the edge of a northern marshland. Thatched wooden dwellings and a gray sea lie behind him, and his hand is raised in blessing.

beats.text: Willehad was born in Northumbria, in England, and in the eighth century became a missionary to the Frisians and Saxons.
About the year seven sixty-six, he went to Frisia to continue the work of Boniface, who had been martyred there.
beats.scene: An icon of Saint Willehad, in a monk's robe, preaching to a small crowd of Frisian villagers in a flat, windswept landscape of low turf-roofed houses and reed-lined waterways under a wide sky.

beats.text: Charlemagne sent him to the Saxons. After two years, they rebelled, and a number of his friends were killed.
beats.scene: An icon of Saint Willehad on a road at the edge of a Saxon forest, a small group of missionaries in dark robes gathered close behind him, under a heavy sky.

beats.text: Willehad fled, and went to Rome to report to the pope. Then he withdrew to the monastery of Echternach. For two years he worked in its scriptorium, and gathered his missionary team.
beats.scene: An icon of Saint Willehad seated at a slanted desk in a Carolingian monastery scriptorium, with parchment and pens before him. Round-arched windows let in soft light, and a few younger monks work beside him.

beats.text: In seven eighty-seven he became bishop of Bremen, and built its cathedral. It was dedicated in seven eighty-nine, the year he died. His holiness was the patience to begin again.
beats.scene: An icon of Saint Willehad as bishop, in mitre and vestments, holding a small model of his cathedral. A modest northern town and the River Weser lie behind him.

beats.text: May we, too, begin again. Saint Willehad, pray for us.

claims.claim: Willehad was a Christian missionary and became Bishop of Bremen in 787.
He was born in Northumbria, and probably educated at York under Ecgbert.
He was a friend of Alcuin.
About 766 he went to Frisia to continue the missionary work of Boniface, who was martyred by the Frisians in 754.
He preached at Dokkum and in Overijssel.
At Paderborn in 777 Saxony was divided into missionary zones, and the zone called Wigmodia, between the Weser and the Elbe, was given to Willehad.
From 780 he preached in the lower Weser region on commission from Charlemagne.
He barely escaped with his life when the Frisians wanted to kill him, and again when local pagans wanted to kill him and his companions for destroying temples.
Charlemagne sent him to evangelize the Saxons; he preached to them for two years.
In 782 the Saxons under Widukind rebelled against Charlemagne, Willehad fled to Frisia, and a number of his assistants and friends were killed.
He traveled to Rome and reported on his work to Pope Adrian I.
He then retired to the monastery of Echternach, where for two years he worked in the scriptorium and reassembled his missionary team.
In 787 he was consecrated bishop and chose Bremen as his see.
He built a cathedral at Bremen, dedicated in 789, and a small church at Blexen.
He died at Blexen on 8 November 789 and is buried in Bremen's cathedral.
Anschar wrote a life of Willehad, whose preface was considered a masterpiece for its age, and praised the cathedral's beauty.
In 860 a sick girl from Wege traveled to his grave and was reportedly cured.

story: Willehad was born in Northumbria, in the north of England, around the year 745. He probably received his education at York, under Ecgbert, and he counted Alcuin among his friends. Little else is recorded of his early years. After his ordination, he turned to missionary work.

About the year 766, Willehad went to Frisia, on the North Sea coast of the continent. He came to continue the mission of Boniface, who had been martyred by the Frisians in 754. It was not a place that promised a warm welcome. Willehad preached at Dokkum and in Overijssel, following in the footsteps of a man who had died doing the same work.

The work was slow and dangerous. At an assembly in Paderborn in 777, the lands of the Saxons were divided into missionary zones, and the region between the Weser and the Elbe, called Wigmodia, was given to Willehad. From 780 he preached in the lower Weser region on commission from Charlemagne. Twice in these years he barely escaped with his life. Once it was the Frisians who wanted to kill him, and he returned to the area around Utrecht. Another time, local pagans wanted to kill him and his fellow missionaries for destroying some of their temples.

Charlemagne then sent him to evangelize the Saxons, and for two years Willehad preached among them. Then, in 782, the Saxons rose in revolt against Charlemagne under their leader Widukind. Willehad had to flee to Frisia. A number of his assistants and friends were killed. The sources do not describe his grief, and we will not invent it. We can only say that a missionary's life is lived among people, and he had lost some of the people he worked beside.

What he did next is worth noticing. He did not simply return to the field. He traveled to Rome and reported on his work to Pope Adrian I. Then he retired for a time to the monastery of Echternach, in present-day Luxembourg. For two years he worked in the scriptorium, and he used that quiet time to reassemble his missionary team. It was a season of stillness and preparation, between the failures behind him and the work ahead.

After Charlemagne's conquest of the Saxons, Willehad went back to preach around the lower Elbe and the lower Weser. In 787 he was consecrated bishop, and the part of Saxony and Friesland near the mouth of the Weser was assigned to him as his diocese. He chose the city of Bremen as his see, and there he built a cathedral. Anschar, who later wrote his life, praised it for its beauty. It was dedicated in 789. Willehad also built a small church at Blexen, on the Weser.

He died at Blexen on 8 November 789, shortly after the cathedral he had built was consecrated, and he was buried in it. His death was not a martyrdom, but the end of a long labor. Anschar's Life of Willehad survives, and its preface was considered a masterpiece for that age. Tradition adds one more note to his story. In 860, a sick girl from the village of Wege, now Weyhe, traveled to his grave and was reportedly cured. That account is also the first time her village appears in any historical document. Willehad is remembered as a man who was driven out more than once and returned each time, and who left behind a church and a city's cathedral.

es.name: San Willehad
es.hook: Perdió a amigos, huyó para salvar la vida y, aun así, volvió a su labor.
es.summary: San Willehad, misionero northumbrio, sobrevivió a amenazas y a una revuelta sajona, luego reconstruyó su misión y llegó a ser obispo de Bremen.
story: Willehad nació en Northumbria, en el norte de Inglaterra, hacia el año 745. Probablemente recibió su formación en York, bajo Egberto, y contó entre sus amigos a Alcuino. De sus primeros años se conserva poca información más. Después de su ordenación, se dedicó a la labor misionera.

Hacia el año 766, Willehad fue a Frisia, en la costa del Mar del Norte, en el continente. Llegó para continuar la misión de Bonifacio, quien había sido martirizado por los frisones en el 754. No era un lugar que prometiera una acogida cálida. Willehad predicó en Dokkum y en Overijssel, siguiendo los pasos de un hombre que había muerto realizando la misma labor.

La obra fue lenta y peligrosa. En una asamblea celebrada en Paderborn en el 777, las tierras de los sajones se dividieron en zonas misionales, y la región entre el Weser y el Elba, llamada Wigmodia, se encomendó a Willehad. Desde el 780 predicó en la zona baja del Weser por encargo de Carlomagno. En esos años estuvo dos veces a punto de perder la vida. Una vez fueron los frisones quienes quisieron matarlo, y regresó a los alrededores de Utrecht. Otra vez, paganos del lugar quisieron matarlo a él y a sus compañeros misioneros por haber destruido algunos de sus templos.

Carlomagno lo envió después a evangelizar a los sajones, y durante dos años Willehad predicó entre ellos. Luego, en el 782, los sajones se levantaron en revuelta contra Carlomagno bajo su caudillo Widukind. Willehad tuvo que huir a Frisia. Varios de sus auxiliares y amigos fueron asesinados. Las fuentes no describen su dolor, y nosotros no lo vamos a inventar. Solo podemos decir que la vida de un misionero transcurre entre personas, y él había perdido a algunas de las personas con quienes trabajaba codo a codo.

Lo que hizo a continuación merece atención. No volvió simplemente al campo de misión. Viajó a Roma e informó de su labor al papa Adriano I. Después se retiró durante un tiempo al monasterio de Echternach, en la actual Luxemburgo. Durante dos años trabajó en el scriptorium y aprovechó ese tiempo de quietud para reorganizar su equipo misionero. Fue una época de calma y preparación, entre los fracasos que quedaban atrás y la labor que le esperaba.

Tras la conquista de los sajones por Carlomagno, Willehad regresó a predicar por la zona baja del Elba y del Weser. En el 787 fue consagrado obispo, y la parte de Sajonia y Frisia cercana a la desembocadura del Weser le fue asignada como diócesis. Eligió la ciudad de Bremen como sede y allí construyó una catedral. Anscario, que más tarde escribió su vida, alabó su belleza. Fue dedicada en el 789. Willehad también construyó una pequeña iglesia en Blexen, junto al Weser.

Murió en Blexen el 8 de noviembre del 789, poco después de que se consagrara la catedral que había construido, y fue enterrado en ella. Su muerte no fue un martirio, sino el final de una larga labor. Se conserva la Vida de Willehad, escrita por Anscario, cuyo prólogo fue considerado una obra maestra para aquella época. La tradición añade una nota más a su historia. En el 860, una niña enferma de la aldea de Wege, hoy Weyhe, viajó hasta su tumba y, según se relata, quedó curada. Ese relato es también la primera vez que su aldea aparece en un documento histórico. Willehad es recordado como un hombre que fue expulsado en más de una ocasión y que regresó cada vez, y que dejó tras de sí una iglesia y la catedral de una ciudad.
es.prayer: Que también nosotros volvamos a empezar. San Willehad, ruega por nosotros.
